newsitem.title: USA: U.S. property-casualty 1996 net income up 17 pct.
newsitem.headline: U.S. property-casualty 1996 net income up 17 pct.

text.p: The U.S. property-casualty insurance industry's consolidated after-tax net income rose 17 percent in 1996 to $24.1 billion, reflecting an increase in realized capital gains and a decrease in catastrophe losses, industry trade groups said.
The industry's realized capital gains rose nearly 60 percent, or $3.6 billion, in 1996 to $9.6 billion. Catastrophe losses fell $960 million to $7.35 billion in 1996.
Without those gains, after-tax income would have declined in 1996, Sean Mooney, senior vice president and economist at the Insurance Information Institute said.
The figures were released by the Insurance Services Office (ISO) and the National Association of Independent Insurers.
They are consolidated estimates for the entire industry based on the reports of insurers that account for 96 percent of the nation's property-casualty insurance business.
The industry's rate of return, calculated on a statutory accounting basis, also showed improvement, rising to 9.4 percent in 1996 from 9.0 percent a year ago.
And although pre-tax operating income rose 3.6 percent in 1996 to $20.2 billion, it consisted of an underwriting loss of $16.8 billion and net investment income of $37.6 billion.
The underwriting loss declined by 4.9 percent in 1996 while the net investment income, primarily dividends earned from stocks and interest on bonds, rose two percent.
Net written premiums for 1996 totaled $268.8 billion, up 3.5 percent, about in line with the 1994 and 1995 growth rates.
Consolidated surplus, assets minus liabilities, rose 11.5 percent to $256.5 billion as of year-end 1996.
In the fourth quarter, the industry's consolidated net income was $7.2 billion compared with net income of $5.5 billion in the 1995 quarter.
Pre-tax operating income rose to $6.4 billion in the fourth quarter of 1996, up from $4.1 billion in the 1995 quarter.
The operating income consisted of a pre-tax underwriting loss of $3.5 billion, down 32.7 percent, and pre-tax net investment income of $10.4 billion, up 10.8 percent.
The improvement in the underwriting results coincided with a drop in catastrophe losses to $895 million in the 1996 fourth quarter, down from $2.6 billion in the 1995 fourth quarter.
Realized capital gains were $2.7 billion in the 1996 fourth quarter.

Fourth quarter written premiums totaled $65.6 billion, up 4.7 percent in the year ago quarter, compared with fourth quarter written premium growth rates of 3.4 percent in 1995 and 2.9 percent in 1994.
